title: Chemical Bonding and Structure
lines: Bonding explains why salt melts at 801 °C while ice melts at 0 °C. Exam questions ask you to name the bond type, draw or judge an electron-dot structure, predict a shape, decide polarity, and link structure to melting point, hardness and conductivity.
## Ionic bonds
- An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. Typical: NaCl, MgO, CaF₂, K₂S.
- Compounds containing NH₄⁺ (such as NH₄Cl) are ionic even though they contain no metal. AlCl₃ is covalent even though it contains a metal.
- Ionic compounds: high melting points, hard but brittle, conduct when molten or dissolved, not when solid.
- Lattice strength grows with ion charge and falls with ion size: MgO (2+, 2−) melts far higher than NaCl (1+, 1−); NaF > NaCl > NaBr in melting point.
> Example: Which has the higher melting point, CaO or KCl?
> CaO has ions of charge 2+ and 2−; KCl has 1+ and 1−. Higher charges and similar sizes give stronger attraction, so CaO melts higher (about 2600 °C against about 770 °C).
## Covalent bonds
- A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms, usually non-metals. Single (H–H), double (O=O), triple (N≡N).
- Non-polar covalent bonds join identical atoms (H–H, Cl–Cl, C–C). Polar covalent bonds join different atoms (H–Cl, O–H); the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge.
- Bond strength: triple > double > single between the same atoms; shorter bonds are stronger. Bond strength decides the thermal stability of molecules: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
- Covalent compounds: acids (HCl, H₂SO₄), non-metal oxides and hydrides, and most organic compounds.
- Coordinate (dative) bonds: both shared electrons come from one atom, as in NH₄⁺ (from NH₃'s lone pair to H⁺) and H₃O⁺. Once formed, the four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are identical.

! Trap: a compound that contains any ionic bond is ionic. NaOH contains an ionic bond and a polar O–H bond; Na₂O₂ contains ionic bonds and a non-polar O–O bond; NH₄Cl contains ionic, polar covalent and coordinate bonds.
## Metallic bonds
- In a metal, positive ions sit in a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move. This explains conductivity of heat and electricity, malleability, ductility and lustre.
- Metallic bond strength rises with more valence electrons and smaller ions: Na < Mg < Al in melting point; Li > Na > K down group 1.
## Electron-dot (Lewis) structures
- Show outer-shell electrons as dots (or crosses) around each symbol. Most atoms reach 8 outer electrons (2 for H).
- For ions, put the ion in square brackets with its charge: [Na]⁺ and [:Cl:]⁻ with eight electrons around Cl. For MgCl₂ draw one Mg²⁺ between two separate Cl⁻ ions, never Cl⁻ merged together.
- Covalent examples: H₂O has two bond pairs and two lone pairs on O; NH₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair; CO₂ is O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O; N₂ is N≡N with one lone pair on each N.
> Example: How many lone pairs and bonding pairs are in a CO₂ molecule?
> Each C=O double bond is 2 shared pairs, so 4 bonding pairs in total. Each O keeps 2 lone pairs, so 4 lone pairs in total. Carbon has none.
! Trap: in HClO the atom order is H–O–Cl, not H–Cl–O, because O needs two bonds. In CCl₄ remember the 3 lone pairs on each Cl; dropping them is the most common mistake in dot-structure options.

- Molecules where some atom does not reach 8: BF₃ (B has 6), BeCl₂ (Be has 4); PCl₅ and SF₆ exceed 8. Questions asking "which molecule has every atom with 8 outer electrons" usually reject these. CO₂, PCl₃, CCl₄ and N₂ pass; H₂O fails only because H has 2.
## Molecular shapes (VSEPR basics)
- Electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible. Count pairs: bonding pairs + lone pairs, treating a double or triple bond as one region.
- 2 regions: linear, 180° (CO₂, BeCl₂, C₂H₂).
- 3 regions: trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃, SO₃, C₂H₄ around each carbon). With one lone pair: bent (SO₂).
- 4 regions: tetrahedral, 109°28′ (CH₄, CCl₄, NH₄⁺). One lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (NH₃, H₃O⁺). Two lone pairs: bent, about 104.5° (H₂O).
- Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so angles shrink: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5°.
- Lone pairs on the central atom = (central atom's outer electrons − electrons used for bonding) / 2, where each bonded H or Cl uses 1 and each O (double bond) uses 2.
> Example: Predict the shape of SO₂.
> S has 6 outer electrons; each O takes 2, so 6 − 4 = 2 electrons remain, one lone pair. Regions: 2 bonds + 1 lone pair = 3, so the shape is bent (V-shaped), less than 120°.
> Example: Predict the shape of NH₃ and of BF₃.
> N: 5 − 3 = 2 electrons, one lone pair; 4 regions, so trigonal pyramidal. B: 3 − 3 = 0, no lone pair; 3 regions, so trigonal planar.
## Polarity of molecules
- A molecule is polar if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetrical molecules with polar bonds can still be non-polar.
- Non-polar: H₂, O₂, N₂, CO₂, CH₄, CCl₄, BF₃, C₂H₄, benzene. Polar: HCl, H₂O, NH₃, SO₂, CH₃Cl, CHCl₃, ethanol.
- Quick rule for ABₙ: if the central atom has no lone pair and all outer atoms are the same, the molecule is non-polar.
- "Like dissolves like": polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents (NH₃ and HCl in water); non-polar in non-polar (I₂ in CCl₄, Br₂ in benzene).
! Trap: CO₂ has polar C=O bonds yet is non-polar; H₂O₂ is polar. Do not decide polarity from bond type alone.
## Intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding

- Van der Waals forces act between all molecules; they are much weaker than chemical bonds. They grow with molar mass for similar molecules: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ in boiling point, and CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄.
- Hydrogen bonds form when H bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on another N, O or F. They are stronger than van der Waals forces but weaker than covalent bonds.

- Effects: H₂O, HF and NH₃ boil far higher than expected for their size (H₂O 100 °C vs H₂S −60 °C). Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open network. Ethanol and NH₃ mix very well with water.
- Melting and boiling of molecular substances break intermolecular forces only; covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact. Stability (decomposition) depends on covalent bond strength.
> Example: Why does H₂O decompose only above 2000 °C but boil at 100 °C?
> Boiling separates molecules (hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces). Decomposition must break strong O–H covalent bonds.
! Trap: hydrogen bonds do not explain why HF is more stable than HCl; that is bond strength. Hydrogen bonds explain why HF boils higher than HCl.
## Crystal types and their properties
- Ionic crystals (NaCl, CsCl, MgO): ions held by ionic bonds; high melting point, brittle, conduct only when molten or dissolved. In NaCl each ion is surrounded by 6 of the other; in CsCl by 8.
- Molecular crystals (ice, dry ice, I₂, S₈, solid noble gases, most organic solids): molecules held by intermolecular forces; low melting points, soft, non-conducting.

- Covalent network (atomic) crystals (diamond, Si, SiO₂, SiC): a giant 3D network of covalent bonds; very high melting points, very hard, insoluble, usually non-conducting (Si is a semiconductor). In diamond each C bonds to 4 others; in SiO₂ each Si bonds to 4 O and each O to 2 Si, and there are no SiO₂ molecules.
- Metallic crystals: metal ions and delocalised electrons; conduct in both solid and liquid states, melting points vary widely (Hg liquid, W about 3400 °C).

- Graphite is a layered (mixed) crystal: strong covalent bonds within layers, weak forces between layers, delocalised electrons that conduct along layers. It is soft and slippery yet has a melting point higher than diamond's.
- Typical melting order: covalent network > ionic > molecular, with metals spread across the range.
> Example: Rank by melting point: SiO₂, NaCl, CO₂, Na.
> SiO₂ (network) > NaCl (ionic, 801 °C) > Na (metallic, 98 °C) > CO₂ (molecular, sublimes at −78 °C).
! Memory trick: "CO₂ is a gas, SiO₂ is sand." Same group, same formula type, completely different crystal type, which is a favourite comparison.
